title: How Live-Stream Interactivity Shapes Cross-Border Purchase Intention: The Serial Mediation of Social Presence and Trust and the Moderating Role of Perceived Platform Security
content: Cross-border live-streaming commerce has become a widely adopted channel through which overseas sellers reach geographically dispersed consumers, yet evidence on how the interactive features of a live room convert into cross-border buying intention remains fragmented. Drawing on the stimulus-organism-response framework, this study develops a moderated serial mediation model in which live-stream interactivity serves as the external stimulus, social presence and trust operate as sequential organism states, and perceived platform security moderates the trust-to-intention path. Survey data from 398 consumers with cross-border live-stream viewing experience were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling. Interactivity positively predicted social presence, social presence positively predicted trust, and trust positively predicted cross-border purchase intention. The serial indirect path through social presence and trust was significant while the direct interactivity-intention path remained significant, indicating partial mediation. Perceived platform security strengthened the trust-to-intention relationship. The study extends the stimulus-organism-response logic to cross-border live retail, clarifies the chained psychological transmission from interactive cues to buying intention, and offers guidance for interaction design and security communication on cross-border platforms.
